### A step is the cheapest interrogation of a dynamic system {#sec-t2-why-step}

[T1](../T1-temperature-static/index.qmd) calibrated two sensors against a
reference thermometer, holding each bath point until nothing moved. Every
number it produced was a *static* one, and every one of them assumed the
sensor had finished responding.

This experiment removes that assumption. Plunge a sensor from one medium into
another and its reading does not jump: it approaches the new temperature over
a time set by how fast heat crosses into it. A step is the cheapest possible
interrogation of that behaviour — one action, no instrumentation beyond what
T1 already used, and a response that contains the whole first-order dynamics.

### The first-order model {#sec-t2-first-order}

Treat the sensor as a lump of material at a single temperature $T$, exchanging
heat with a medium at $T_\infty$ through a surface $A$ with convection
coefficient $h$. Conservation of energy gives

$$
\rho c V \frac{\mathrm{d}T}{\mathrm{d}t} = hA\left(T_\infty - T\right)
$$ {#eq-t2-ode}

whose solution from an initial $T_0$ is the exponential approach

$$
T(t) = T_\infty + \left(T_0 - T_\infty\right)e^{-t/\tau},
\qquad
\tau = \frac{\rho c V}{hA}
$$ {#eq-t2-step}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
The lumped assumption — one temperature for the whole sensor — is what makes
@eq-t2-ode first order, and it is exactly what fails for the sheathed probe of
@sec-t2-second-order. Its validity is usually stated through the Biot number
$\mathrm{Bi} = hL_c/k$, with $L_c$ a characteristic length and $k$ the
sensor's own thermal conductivity: below about $0.1$ the internal gradient is
negligible and one lump is enough. A bare thermistor bead in air is
comfortably in that regime; the same bead inside a stainless sheath is not.
:::

**$\tau$ is a property of the sensor *and* the medium together**, not of the
sensor alone. The same probe has a $\tau$ in still air tens of times larger
than in stirred water, because $h$ changes by that factor while $\rho c V$
does not. A datasheet quoting "response time" without naming the medium is
quoting nothing.

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
### Fitting $\tau$ {#sec-t2-fit}
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Fitting $\tau$ (1)
:::

Two routes, and the choice matters.

**Linearised.** Rearranging @eq-t2-step,

$$
\ln\left|T(t) - T_\infty\right| = \ln\left|T_0 - T_\infty\right| - \frac{t}{\tau}
$$ {#eq-t2-linearised}

is a straight line whose slope is $-1/\tau$, fitted by ordinary least squares.
It is quick, and it is what a hurried analysis reaches for.

**Nonlinear.** Fit $T_\infty$, $T_0$ and $\tau$ of @eq-t2-step directly by
least squares on the residuals in temperature.

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
### Fitting $\tau$ (2)
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## The linearised fit is not the same fit

Taking the logarithm compresses the tail and stretches nothing, so equal
weight in $\ln|T-T_\infty|$ is *unequal* weight in $T$: the last few samples,
where $T - T_\infty$ is a few millikelvin and almost entirely noise,
dominate the slope. Worse, $T_\infty$ must be assumed before the line can be
drawn, and any error in it curves the supposed straight line — which is then
usually blamed on the sensor.

This template fits @eq-t2-step **nonlinearly**, estimating $T_\infty$ along
with $\tau$, and shows the linearised fit alongside so the difference is
visible rather than asserted.
:::

### From $\tau$ to the convection coefficient {#sec-t2-h}

Rearranging the definition in @eq-t2-step,

$$
h = \frac{\rho c V}{\tau A}
$$ {#eq-t2-h}

so a measured $\tau$, plus the sensor's own thermal mass, estimates $h$ for
that medium. The thermal mass $\rho c V$ and the area $A$ are properties of
the probe, identical across media, so the **ratio** of two media's
coefficients,

$$
\frac{h_2}{h_1} = \frac{\tau_1}{\tau_2}
$$ {#eq-t2-h-ratio}

needs no probe geometry at all — which is fortunate, because
$\rho c V/A$ for a real encapsulated sensor is not something a laboratory can
easily know. Report the ratios as measurements and any absolute $h$ as an
estimate resting on a stated $\rho c V/A$.

### Ramp input: the error that never goes away {#sec-t2-ramp}

A step is a laboratory idealisation. A real process often ramps. Substituting
$T_\infty(t) = T_0 + \dot{T}t$ into @eq-t2-ode and solving, the transient dies
and what remains is a constant lag:

$$
e_\infty = T(t) - T_\infty(t) \longrightarrow -\tau\dot{T}
$$ {#eq-t2-ramp}

The sensor reads **low by $\tau\dot{T}$**, for ever, and no amount of waiting
improves it. This is the single most practically useful result in the
experiment: a $\tau$ of 2.5 s on a bath ramping at $0.5\,\mathrm{K\,s^{-1}}$
is a steady $1.25$ K error that a static calibration would never reveal, and
that averaging makes *more* confident rather than smaller.

### Second order: what a sheath does {#sec-t2-second-order}

A sheathed probe is two lumps — the sheath, and the element inside it — in
series. Its step response is the sum of two exponentials,

$$
T(t) = T_\infty + \left(T_0 - T_\infty\right)
\left[\frac{\tau_1 e^{-t/\tau_1} - \tau_2 e^{-t/\tau_2}}{\tau_1 - \tau_2}\right]
$$ {#eq-t2-second-order}

and the signature is at the very beginning: a first-order response has its
**maximum slope at $t = 0$**, while this one starts with zero slope and
inflects. The element cannot feel the medium until the sheath has warmed.

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
A first-order fit to second-order data does not fail loudly. It returns a
plausible $\tau$ and a residual that looks small — until it is plotted against
time, where it shows a clear arc: negative early, positive through the middle,
negative again. That shape, not the residual's magnitude, is the diagnostic,
and it is why every fit in this experiment is followed by a residual plot
rather than by a single goodness number.
:::

### Reading temperature at all {#sec-t2-calibration}

Nothing above can be done in volts. Each record must first be converted to
temperature, and the conversion is [T1](../T1-temperature-static/index.qmd)'s:
invert the divider or the bridge for the sensor's resistance, then apply the
Steinhart–Hart or Callendar–Van Dusen curve **fitted in T1**, not a datasheet
one.

This is the first experiment on this site whose result depends on an earlier
experiment's calibration, and it is worth noticing what that implies: T1's fit
residuals and T1's own uncertainty propagate into every $\tau$ measured here,
and appear in the budget as a component. A calibration is not a one-off
ceremony; it is an input quantity with an uncertainty, used downstream.
